**Reading time:** about 4 minutes. **Goal:** discover the themes associated with Plato's later writings without treating a disputed chronology as his personal diary.

Plato returned from his last reported visit to Sicily around **360 BC**. He was in his late sixties and remained closely connected with the **Academy** in Athens until his death in **348/347 BC**. Our knowledge of his ordinary activities during these years is limited. We cannot reconstruct a teaching timetable or identify exactly when each surviving dialogue was written.

What we can examine is the philosophical work associated with his later period. These dialogues show new ways of organizing discussions about knowledge, being, political rule and the natural world. They do not amount to a simple story in which an older Plato abandons all his earlier ideas.

## Which dialogues are late?

Scholars often classify Plato's works as **early, middle and late**, drawing in part on differences in the style of the Greek prose. This is a useful guide, not a calendar of composition.

A group commonly regarded as late includes the *Sophist*, *Statesman*, *Philebus*, *Timaeus*, *Critias* and *Laws*. The *Theaetetus* and *Parmenides*, also important for understanding the questions pursued in this phase of Plato's writing, are often placed in an **intermediate group**. Their exact relation in time to other dialogues remains debated.

The classification does not prove precisely what Plato believed at a particular age. A philosophical problem can be explored, reconsidered or dramatized in more than one work.

## New questions, new speakers

Some dialogues associated with the later group give **Socrates a smaller role**. In the *Sophist* and *Statesman*, a visitor from Elea guides much of the inquiry; in the *Timaeus*, a different speaker offers a sustained account of the universe. In the *Laws*, Socrates does not appear.

This change in dramatic form matters. Rather than presenting one unvarying “Socratic method,” Plato gives different characters different ways of reasoning. The *Sophist* investigates being and not-being, while the *Statesman* asks what knowledge is needed to govern well. The *Philebus* examines pleasure, understanding and the good life.

## Revisiting difficult problems

The *Parmenides* presents demanding objections to the account of Forms voiced by a young Socrates. These objections are serious, but their presence in the dialogue does not tell us by itself whether Plato had rejected the Forms or was investigating problems any adequate theory must face.

The *Timaeus* turns to the **order of the cosmos** and the relation between intelligible patterns and the changing world. Its speaker offers an account whose status and limits are themselves part of the philosophical discussion. Plato's inquiry extends beyond political life and ethics without leaving those concerns behind.

These works invite readers to see philosophy not as a collection of finished doctrines, but as an activity capable of testing its own explanations.

## The Laws and political thought

The *Laws*, Plato's longest dialogue, describes the institutions and education of a proposed city. It differs in important respects from the city discussed in the *Republic*, and gives detailed attention to legislation and civic practices.

Calling it simply a **“realistic second-best Republic”** risks overlooking the difficult arguments and distinctive purposes of both works. There are reasons to compare them; there is no secure evidence that the *Laws* was written as a direct reaction to failure in Syracuse.

Aristotle indicates that the *Laws* followed the *Republic*. Diogenes Laertius (III 37) reports a tradition that it remained **unfinished or not fully revised** when Plato died and was subsequently handled by **Philip of Opus**. We should preserve the difference between this ancient report and an independently verified publication history.

## The Academy and the people around Plato

Plato remained a central figure in the Academy, where discussion and mathematical inquiry continued. **Aristotle**, who had joined the circle around **367 BC**, remained associated with it during Plato's lifetime; he would later develop his own approach.

After Plato's death, the Academy passed to his nephew **Speusippus**. This succession is better established than stories about Plato's precise final lectures or personal intentions. The differences among members also remind us that the Academy was not an institution in which everyone simply repeated the founder's conclusions.

## A continuing inquiry

In Plato's later works, the questions become no less important: **How can we distinguish knowledge from appearance? What kind of reasoning makes government good? How can we understand a changing universe?**

His last years did not close those questions. They left readers a set of dialogues in which philosophical inquiry remains active, even when an answer seems near.

**Question for the reader:** if a philosopher tests an idea he defended elsewhere, should we call that a contradiction—or an example of thinking seriously?

## Dialogues to explore

- *Parmenides* — difficulties concerning the Forms; not securely dated to Plato's very last years.
- *Theaetetus* — what knowledge might be.
- *Sophist* — being, not-being and philosophical method.
- *Statesman* — knowledge, law and political expertise.
- *Philebus* — pleasure and understanding in the good life.
- *Timaeus* and *Critias* — the cosmos and the unfinished continuation of its dramatic setting.
- *Laws* — legislation and education in a proposed city; probably among Plato's final works.

## Sources and historical orientation

- Aristotle, *Politics* II 6, 1264b24–27 — the *Laws* composed after the *Republic*.
- Diogenes Laertius, *Lives of Eminent Philosophers* III 37 — later tradition about the state of the *Laws*.
- *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy*, “Plato” and “Plato's Laws” — dialogue chronology, interpretive disagreements and the ancient testimony.
- Leonard Brandwood, “Stylometry and Chronology,” in *The Cambridge Companion to Plato* — stylistic evidence and its limits.
- Malcolm Schofield, “Plato in His Time and Place,” in Gail Fine (ed.), *The Oxford Handbook of Plato*, 2nd ed. (Oxford University Press, 2019), pp. 55, 60–64 — the Academy and later dialogues.
